nameStory: Like other fishing spiders, Dolomedes striatus gets its common name from its remarkable ability to hunt on water surfaces, literally fishing for aquatic prey. The scientific name 'striatus' means 'striped' in Latin, referring to the distinctive banded patterns that help distinguish this species from its fishing spider cousins.
description: The striped fishing spider is a large, semi-aquatic hunter that can walk on water with remarkable grace. These impressive spiders have robust, hairy bodies with distinctive striped patterns running along their legs and abdomen. They're quite substantial in size, with females reaching up to an inch in body length, while males are typically smaller and more slender.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for clear striped patterns on the legs and body - these bands are usually light and dark alternating stripes that feel slightly raised when touched gently

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Robust, stocky build with a distinctly hairy texture that feels almost fuzzy - the dense hairs help repel water and trap air bubbles

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females have bodies roughly the size of a large grape, with legs that can span across your palm - males are noticeably smaller and more delicate

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen skating across water surfaces with legs spread wide, or hanging head-down near water edges with front legs touching the surface to detect vibrations

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds no hunting web - instead creates silken nursery webs in vegetation near water that feel papery and are often visible as white, tent-like structures

habitat: Found along the edges of ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and boggy areas throughout New England's lowlands. They prefer areas with emergent vegetation like cattails, sedges, and overhanging shrubs that provide both hunting perches and shelter. Look for them in quiet backwaters rather than fast-flowing streams.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots under logs and rocks near water. Mating activity begins as temperatures warm, with males becoming more active and visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen hunting on water surfaces. Females create distinctive white nursery webs in waterside vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue hunting until first frost, with spiderlings dispersing from nursery webs. Late-season individuals seek overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under bark, logs, or rock crevices near water. They become completely inactive and are rarely encountered.

funFact: When threatened while on water, striped fishing spiders can actually dive underwater and stay submerged for up to 30 minutes by trapping air bubbles in their dense body hairs - essentially carrying their own scuba tank!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fishing spiders, especially the dark fishing spider. Remember: if you see clear stripes on the legs and body, think 'striatus.' Dark fishing spiders have more mottled, less defined patterns and tend to be darker overall.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fishing' spiders, they don't use hooks or lines - the name comes from their ability to catch small fish, tadpoles, and aquatic insects by detecting surface vibrations with their legs, much like an angler feeling for a bite.
compareHints: Among New England's fishing spiders, striatus has the most clearly defined striped patterns - other species like the dark fishing spider have more mottled or spotted appearances. The six-spotted fishing spider has distinct white spots rather than stripes, while the white-banded fishing spider has broader, more prominent white bands rather than fine stripes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the striped fishing spider and six-spotted fishing spider which are typically found near water and have more contrasting markings, the dark fishing spider has subtler coloration and lives almost exclusively on trees.

Among New England's fishing spiders, the Striped Fishing Spider is distinguished by its pale brown coloration with prominent light stripes, while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker and larger, and the Six-spotted Fishing Spider has distinctive white spots instead of stripes.
The six-spotted fishing spider is distinguished from its close relative the Dark Fishing Spider by its characteristic six light spots versus the Dark Fishing Spider's white side stripes.
Among New England's fishing spiders, the Banded Fishing Spider is distinguished by its bold, regular light bands across a dark body.

The white-banded fishing spider stands out from its fishing spider relatives by having the most clearly defined white bands - the dark fishing spider has more subdued, mottled markings, while the striped fishing spider shows yellowish stripes rather than bright white bands.
